title: Computer aided functional style identifcation and correction in modern Russian texts
short_title: Functional Style Identification and Correction in Modern Russian

affiliations.2: Department of Cancer Biology, Cancer Institute, University College London, London, UK

journal: Journal of Data, Information and Management
abstract: Functional style (FS) identification is a classification task in linguistics that categorizes unrestricted texts into several categories of linguistic norms. FS is widely used to attain a satisfying outcome in style processing. As such, we train a deep learning attention neural network model on modern-Russian texts, divide them into four FS categories. The model obtained an accuracy of 0.72. In particular, 81.08% and 85.71% accuracy in classifying the artistic and academic FS. The proposed model is able to automate the FS identification process and aids both domain experts and non-domain experts to perform FS correction by highlighting style anomalies concerning a desired style for the text. In particular, we show a 34% and 31% average improvement in the duration of performing the style correction task. Moreover, domain experts and non-domain experts obtain 3% and 9% more accurate results, respectively.
summary: Functional style describes which set of linguistic norms a text follows, such as artistic or academic writing. We trained a deep learning attention neural network to sort modern Russian texts into four functional styles, reaching 0.72 accuracy, and used it to highlight style anomalies so people can correct a text toward a desired style. With the tool, style correction time improved by 34% and 31% on average, and domain experts and non-experts were 3% and 9% more accurate.
key_findings: The attention neural network classified modern Russian texts into four functional styles with an accuracy of 0.72.
Accuracy reached 81.08% for the artistic style and 85.71% for the academic style.
Highlighting style anomalies gave 34% and 31% average improvements in the time needed to perform style correction.
Domain experts and non-domain experts obtained 3% and 9% more accurate results, respectively.
